Senses.Explanation: The verdict “toil, yet no result” (勞而無功) is applied in Chan records to fruitless searching, speaking, contrivance, and failed responses. Zhantang Wenzhun answers “I do not understand” with “toil without result.” Another retained address warns that pursuing outside objects spends effort without result. Verses and addresses use the same four graphs where exertion is expressly followed by failure to accomplish; the phrase judges the outcome of the labor, not labor as such.

Senses.Explanation: The verb describes distinct positions, faculties, objects, or roles entering into reciprocal relation without necessarily losing their places. Shitou Xiqian’s verse asks whether every object at every gate mutually interchanges or does not, then says that in interchange they enter into one another and otherwise remain in position (回而更相涉，不爾依位住). Yongjue Yuanxian explicitly explains interchange as faculties and objects entering one another like jewels in Indra’s net, and non-interchange as each remaining in its own position without mixture. Caoshan Benji requires mutual interchange in connection with ordinary feelings and holy views. Eryin Mi says a rigid guest-host distinction still leaves the two mutually awaiting and interchanging, before requiring guest within host and host within guest. Hongzhi Zhengjue joins mutual interchange with side participation, turning the body, and passing breath. Yuanwu Keqin supplies the negative edge, praising an action with “no mutual interchange,” while Baiyu Jingsi preserves a direct question about the mutual interchange of upright and inclined and answers with yesterday’s rain and today’s wind. The term therefore covers reciprocal entry and coordinated shifting, while explicit non-interchange and “no interchange” preserve distinction as a live contrast.

Senses.Explanation: Turn the light back and reflect is a recurrent demand to examine one's own understanding, and the records also use the phrase to expose a counterfeit built from shutting out sights and sounds. Guishan Lingyou tells Yangshan Huiji to turn the light back because nobody else knows Yangshan's understanding, and asks him to present that understanding. Yuanwu Keqin rebukes an audience that will not turn back despite being stopped at every sense gate; Tianyin Yuanxiu tells an assembly not to seek outside; Dahui Zonggao addresses officials absorbed in public business. Zhongfeng Mingben supplies the sharpest limit: he says people who withdraw sight and hearing until they resemble wood and stone falsely call that turning the light back. Jifei Ruyi instead pairs it with tracing the source of the delusive body, while Yuanwu's Essentials tells a student who has been turned by a phrase to turn back and inspect.

Senses.Explanation: A refuse heap is where discarded filth is piled. Chan masters make it a place for burying pretension and rejected words, yet the same corpus pictures a full-sized golden body appearing on its top and a bright pearl found there; the heap does not itself fix the value of what appears on it. A question in the Complete Collection of the Five Lamps contrasts Yunmen’s threat to beat Shakyamuni with a threat to smother Yunmen on a refuse heap; the recorded reply is thirty blows. Zhenjing Kewen says ten or five muddy, indiscriminate fellows like Yunmen could be buried in the refuse heap without fault. Xuedou Chongxian says a full-sized golden body appears atop the refuse heap, then sets the line aside before pressing the case further. Dongshan Shouchu likens his joy to finding a bright pearl on a refuse heap. Shiyu Mingfang says he cast a worn-out whisk onto such a heap for more than ten years. These opposed predicates keep the literal locale stable.

Senses.Explanation: The top of a dung-sweepings heap is the refuse pile where discarded and filthy things collect. Chan masters repeatedly make it the unlikely place where a jewel, treasure, robe, shoe, or even a golden body is found, while also using the same heap for adding still more rubbish. Juelang Daosheng says the Buddha found a mud pellet on the heap and raised it before the assembly. Muting Pufu calls a display of pots, tiles, bamboo scraps, and bricks “adding more rubbish atop the dung heap.” Xuedou Chongxian places a sixteen-foot golden body on the heap before setting that proposition aside. Changling Zhuo’s verse says treasure is found there without seeking. Dongshan Liangjie compares joy after leaving holy truth undone to finding a bright pearl on the heap. Yehai Ziqing says he found a torn robe there and kept it for decades. Mi’an Xianjie uses the rubbish-adding frame after saying that even forgetting both delusion and awakening remains additional refuse.

ActorAttribution.GrammarEvidence: The book title and the record's self-reference 宗堅 identify Doushuai Bulin Zongjian as the sermon speaker carrying the headword.

Senses.Explanation: The phrase denies even the smallest application or yield. Yuanwu answers that the named dust-dust concentration admits no added drop; a rain sermon addresses two months without rain; a third exchange uses it for a dragon blocking every river. Three independent sermons apply the same zero-drop image to nonaddition, drought, and total hydrological obstruction.

Senses.Explanation: The paired transformations describe Yuanwu’s unrestricted ability to elevate, overturn, and reverse valuations. Yuanwu lists them first as the function of Yuanwu’s staff and later as his own staff’s universal activity. The Blue Cliff pointer and Yuanwu’s sermon are distinct uses of the same reversible-transformation image.
